title: Wave 1 prep: shared refactors the whole epic depends on
description:
No behaviour change. Does once what six tickets each budgeted separately:
- Convert every in-tree exhaustive SearchOpts/HybridOpts/RecallOpts literal to ..Default::default(), including benchmarks/ (which just ci does not build).
- Add Hit::new + #[non_exhaustive] on Hit.
- Migrate Nidus::list/Store::list to ListOpts { offset, limit, filter }.
- Extract the RRF fusion tail into src/fuse.rs::rrf_fuse, capturing per-leg score+rank and accepting per-leg weights, behind a golden test written FIRST.
- Clamp TopK::new's pre-allocation — a live panic-on-absurd-top_k that three design agents independently rediscovered.

Turns N*N merges into N one-line additions. See nidus-m50.15 for the decisions this encodes.
close_reason: Closed

title: MCP remember accepts no attrs, so nothing written is ever filterable
description:
The remember tool schema (src/server/mcp.rs) takes collection, text, id, and summarize — and nothing else. There is no way to attach a project, a path, a session, a kind, or a timestamp.

The consequence outlives the tool call: every memory written through MCP is permanently unfilterable, no matter what filtering is added later. This is why it is filed as a bug rather than a feature, and why it blocks the filters-on-recall work — adding filters to recall is pointless while nothing on the write side can be filtered on.

The library and the HTTP upsert path both take a full attrs map already; only the MCP tool drops it.
acceptance_criteria: remember accepts an open attrs map, typed per Value; the schema description tells the model what attrs are for and gives an example (the descriptions drive tool-selection quality); values round-trip to recall results unchanged.

title: MCP over stdio: a 'nidus mcp' subcommand
description:
The MCP service is only mounted inside the HTTP server at /mcp — there is no stdio transport anywhere in src/. So adopting nidus as agent memory means running a server, managing a bearer token, and registering an HTTP endpoint.

The zero-friction path an MCP client expects is a single command: 'claude mcp add nidus -- nidus mcp --dir ~/.nidus'. This is the highest-leverage item on the epic; nothing else here gets used without it.
design: Reuse the existing tool set and the same run_read/run_write helpers rather than forking a second implementation — the difference is the transport, not the surface. Note what the HTTP path provides that stdio does not inherit for free: the body limit, backpressure, and metrics all live in the axum middleware stack the MCP service is nested inside. Decide which of those matter for a single local client and which are honestly unnecessary. Single-process stdio also means the writer lock is held for the session — check the interaction with cross-process readers.
acceptance_criteria: 'nidus mcp --dir DIR' speaks MCP 2026-07-28 over stdio with the full tool set; an e2e test drives the real binary over a pipe, in the existing tests/e2e target; the getting-started docs show the one-line client registration.

title: Filter: array containment predicates over Value::List
description:
`Value::List(Vec<String>)` exists but no predicate can look inside it. Eq compares the whole list; Glob explicitly rejects a list (see the glob_list_value_fails test in src/filter/mod.rs). So tag filtering — the canonical memory-store query, 'tags contains rust' — is impossible today.

turbopuffer has Contains, NotContains, ContainsAny, NotContainsAny, and the element-wise range family AnyLt/AnyLte/AnyGt/AnyGte.

Ships in the first PR alongside nidus boolean composition.
design: Minimum viable set: Contains(key, Value), NotContains, ContainsAny(key, Vec<Value>). The Any* range family is lower value while List is Vec<String> only — revisit once typed arrays exist (see the float/datetime ticket). Decide and document the absent-key and empty-list semantics explicitly, matching how Ne/NotIn already treat a missing attr.
acceptance_criteria: Element containment works over Value::List; absent-key and empty-list behaviour is specified in SPEC.md section 7 and covered by tests; predicates are exposed over HTTP, the CLI, and all three SDKs; the misleading glob_list_value_fails test is updated to point at the new predicate.
close_reason: Shipped in the first PR: Predicate gains All/Any/Not and Contains/NotContains/ContainsAny, purely additive to the wire format.

title: Filter: boolean composition — Or/Not with arbitrary nesting
description:
`Filter(pub Vec<Predicate>)` in src/model.rs is a flat conjunction: an empty filter matches everything, otherwise every predicate must hold. There is no disjunction and no negation of a group, so ordinary queries are inexpressible — 'project = nidus OR project = beads', 'NOT (kind = scratch AND stale = true)'.

turbopuffer has And/Or/Not nested arbitrarily. This is the single filter change that unlocks the most queries per unit of work, and it must land before anything else that serialises a filter.

Ships in the first PR alongside nidus array-containment.
design: `Filter` is a public tuple struct, so moving to a tree is a BREAKING API change — minor bump pre-1.0, and the docs/SDK filter examples move with it. Suggested shape: keep `Filter` as the entry point, make its body an enum (All(Vec)/Any(Vec)/Not(Box)/Pred(Predicate)) so `Filter(vec![p])` stays expressible and the common flat-AND path keeps its current evaluation cost. Serde representation is load-bearing: it is the HTTP /search body and the MCP tool schema, and all three SDKs mirror it.
acceptance_criteria: Or/Not/nested groups evaluate correctly in src/filter/; flat-AND filters keep identical semantics and no measurable slowdown on the scan path; the wire format round-trips through serde; HTTP + all three SDKs accept the new shape; SPEC.md section 7 updated.
close_reason: Shipped in the first PR: Predicate gains All/Any/Not and Contains/NotContains/ContainsAny, purely additive to the wire format.

title: Consolidated SDK + client wiring for every m50 feature
description:
One pass at the end of the epic wiring every m50 addition through the three client SDKs (sdks/js, sdks/go, sdks/python) and their docs, instead of each ticket doing its own slice.

Why batched: the SDK type/client files are touched by nearly every m50 ticket, so per-ticket SDK edits were the single largest merge-conflict source in the epic — and each one costs a full round of three test suites. Doing it once, after the wire format has stopped moving, is cheaper and safer.

Surface to cover (grows as waves land):
- m50.9 text predicates: Fuzzy, ContainsAllTokens, ContainsAnyToken, ContainsTokenSequence, Regex — filter builders in all three SDKs (supersedes nidus-icn).
- m50.7 projection: include_attributes / exclude_attributes.
- m50.12: the per-query exact flag.
- m50.10 multi-field BM25 clauses.
- m50.3 ranking: order_by and decay.
- m50.5 annotations, m50.6 aggregation/limit_per, m50.11 batching.

Note the predicates and request fields already serialize via serde derives, so the JSON wire format works TODAY for a hand-built request — this ticket is the ergonomic builder surface, the typed request/response shapes, and the SDK docs.

Gates: just sdk-go-test, sdk-go-lint, sdk-py-test, sdk-py-lint, sdk-js-test — and sdks/js/package-lock.json must come back unmodified.

title: A large top_k panics instead of returning 400
description:
TopK::new does BinaryHeap::with_capacity(k+1) on a caller-supplied top_k that is clamped nowhere. Reproduced: top_k=usize::MAX/2 panics with 'capacity overflow' from raw_vec.

Severity is bounded but real. Search takes a READ guard and std RwLock only poisons on a write-guard panic, so this does not brick the server; it is a panic where the contract says a bad request is a 400, and it violates SPEC 6.6's graceful-failure discipline (try_reserve, OOM as Err not abort) that the rest of the crate follows carefully.

Three independent design agents rediscovered this while planning unrelated tickets, which is a decent signal it is worth fixing at the boundary rather than per-caller. Fixed in the Wave 1 prep (nidus-m50.16): clamp the pre-allocation to something the store could actually return, and reject an absurd top_k at the DTO boundary.
close_reason: Closed

title: DECISION LOG: the 22 open design questions across the m50 epic
description:
The design pass over m50 surfaced 22 questions whose answers change more than one ticket. Austin delegated them ("pick defaults and keep going"), so they are decided here once rather than re-litigated per ticket. Each is recorded with its reasoning; any can be overturned in review.

CROSS-TICKET
1. Nidus::list takes a ListOpts struct. One break now beats positional growth across .3/.7/.8.
2. #[non_exhaustive] on Hit only. NOT on the opts structs — it would forbid external ..Default::default(), which is the very pattern we are standardizing on.
3. The name search_ranked belongs to .3 (decay). .6 does not rename the existing body.
4. rrf_fuse captures per-leg score+rank AND takes per-leg weights from the start, so .5 and .3a do not reshape it later.
5. MCP knob budget: m50 adds NOTHING to the recall tool. Five tickets each wanted a knob; six on one tool is a tool-selection regression nobody was measuring. New knobs are HTTP/SDK-only.
6. Versions increment in wave order; every bump touches both install snippets.

RANKING (.3)
7. Decay SUBTRACTS: base − lambda*(1 − factor). Multiply would force Cosine-only plus a negative-score clamp; subtract works for every metric and sign.
8. Decay.missing defaults to 1.0 — an un-stamped doc is not penalized, so adding decay never silently buries existing data.
9. rank_by does NOT force the exact path. .12's explicit exact flag is the opt-in; the approximation is documented.
10. Cross-type ORDER BY: mismatched/unorderable values sort into a trailing bucket, mirroring the filter same-type rule.
11. Ranked scans ship serial with a documented performance cliff. Generalizing parallel_topk is its own ticket.

SHAPING (.6, .7, .8)
12. include_attributes + exclude_attributes together is a 400, not a precedence rule.
13. /list gets projection (free once ListOpts exists).
14. limit_per: docs missing the key form ONE shared group, so a missing attribute cannot bypass the cap.
15. Sum reports a tagged Value, consistent with the rest of the API.
16. MAX_GROUPS is a const; limit_per over-fetch multiplier is 8.
17. Pagination caps at 10_000 (const), top_k too, and TopK's total order becomes a stated SPEC contract.
18. RecallOpts gains none of offset/projection/exact — the memory API stays lean.

TEXT (.9, .10, .13)
19. Regex is DROPPED from .9 and filed as its own decision ticket. A new engine is a dependency decision per CLAUDE.md, and hand-rolling an NFA is out of proportion to demand. Fuzzy + token predicates ship.
20. Fuzzy folds ASCII case, following IGlob's precedent.
21. Token predicates look inside Value::List (consistent with Contains). Exceeding MAX_FUZZY_EDITS is a 400, not a silent clamp.
22. .10 uses clauses:[{field,query}] rather than fields:[string]; an empty clause list is a 400; MCP does not see combine; per-clause weights defer to .3.
design: Ordering follows the wave plan from the design synthesis: prep (m50.0) → .8+.13 → .12+.7+.9+.6a → .10+.3a → .5+.6b → .11b+.3b.
notes:
OVERTURNED by the user, 2026-08-07: decision #19 (regex dropped) is reversed. Regex ships, using the widely-used `regex` crate rather than a hand-rolled engine. Its linear-time finite-automata guarantee removes the ReDoS concern that motivated the original deferral, so no timeout guard is needed. Constraint carried forward: the whole-crate clean build must stay well under a minute (CLAUDE.md, CI-asserted), so the build cost is measured before/after and regex-lite is the fallback if the budget breaks.
ADDED 2026-08-07 (user): all client-SDK work across the epic is batched into one consolidated pass at the end (nidus-m50.18) rather than done per ticket. The SDK type/client files are touched by nearly every ticket, so per-ticket edits were the epic's largest merge-conflict source and each cost a full round of three test suites. Library + HTTP + CLI still ship per ticket; only the client libraries defer.

title: MCP write hygiene tools: forget, get, and browse
description:
The tool set is remember, recall, text_search, hybrid_search, list_collections, stats. There is no delete, no get-by-id, and no way to browse what is stored.

Two consequences: a memory that turns out to be wrong can never be corrected or removed, and an agent cannot check what it already knows before storing a near-duplicate. The HTTP layer already has delete, records, and list — this is exposure, not new machinery.
acceptance_criteria: forget (by id, and by filter once filters land), get by id, and a bounded browse/list tool are available over MCP; each routes through the existing run_write/run_read helpers; destructive tools describe their scope unambiguously in the schema so a model does not over-delete.

title: Expose metadata filters on the MCP search tools
description:
recall takes collection, query, top_k, and min_score. text_search and hybrid_search are similarly bare. None of them accepts a filter, even though the library has a full Filter type and POST /search already takes one.

For memory spanning many repos this is the difference between usable and not: an agent needs 'recall X where project = nidus'. Collections as namespaces are too coarse — the useful query unions several scopes with weighting rather than partitioning them.

Blocked on the filter shape landing first (boolean composition + array containment), so the tool schema is written once against the final shape rather than migrated.
acceptance_criteria: recall, text_search, and hybrid_search accept a filter matching the post-rework wire shape; the hand-written JSON schema describes it well enough for a model to construct one unaided; covered in tests/e2e/mcp.rs.

title: Agent memory store: make nidus usable as Claude Code's memory
description:
The MCP surface at /mcp already exposes remember, recall, text_search, hybrid_search, list_collections, and stats with server-side embedding — the search half is largely there. What is missing is plumbing and write hygiene: how a client connects, what a written memory carries, how it is scoped on the way out, and how it is corrected or removed.

Ordering: stdio transport, then attrs on remember, then filters on the search tools, then forget. Those four are what turn this from a vector store with an MCP adapter into something an agent can actually keep memory in.
design: The MCP layer is an adapter (src/server/mcp.rs) — every tool routes through the same run_read/run_write helpers as the HTTP handlers, the tool surface stays text-native (no tool takes a raw vector, asserted by tests/e2e/mcp.rs), and schemas stay hand-written JSON because the descriptions drive tool selection. Every child here holds to that.

title: Value: float and datetime attribute types
description:
`Value` is Null|Str|Int|Bool|List(Vec<String>). Two absences bite:

- No float — a confidence, a score, or any measurement cannot be stored or range-filtered without encoding it as an Int.
- No datetime — recency lives in an epoch Int by convention, which every caller must agree on and nothing enforces.

turbopuffer has string, int, uint, float, uuid, datetime, bool, plus a typed array of each.
design: Float needs an ordering decision for filters (total order over NaN, or reject NaN at the boundary) and an equality decision — document both rather than inheriting IEEE surprises silently. Both variants extend the value codec in src/value.rs, so the on-disk encoding needs a compatibility story: old stores must still open. Typed arrays beyond List(Vec<String>) are a separate, larger change — file separately if wanted.
acceptance_criteria: Float and datetime round-trip through the value codec (tested against in-memory buffers, Miri-clean); range predicates work on both; a store written by the previous version still opens; NaN and timezone handling are specified in SPEC.md.
close_reason: Value::Float(f64) and Value::DateTime(i64) appended last; SDKs, docs and SPEC updated.

title: Ranking expressions: recency decay, attribute ordering, score boosting
description:
nidus offers exactly three rankings: cosine, BM25, or RRF of the two with fixed leg weights. There is no way to boost by an attribute, weight the hybrid legs, decay by age, or plain ORDER BY.

turbopuffer's rank_by covers attribute asc/desc, Product, Sum, Max, Saturate, Decay, and Dist. For a memory store, decay is the one that most changes result quality: on pure cosine a two-year-old note beats a fresh one that says the same thing.
design: Do not import turbopuffer's whole expression language. The high-value subset is (a) time decay over a numeric/datetime attr, (b) a weight per hybrid leg, (c) ORDER BY an attribute with no vector at all. Decay wants a real timestamp type — coordinate with the float/datetime ticket, though an epoch Int is a workable interim.
acceptance_criteria: A recall can be ranked by cosine combined with an age decay; hybrid leg weights are settable; results can be ordered by an attribute without a vector query; every mode is reachable from HTTP and the SDKs.

title: Search parity: close the ranking/filter gaps against turbopuffer
description:
nidus answers three rankings (cosine, BM25, fixed-RRF hybrid) over a flat AND-only filter. A survey against turbopuffer's query surface found the gaps below, ordered by how much each unlocks for the memory use case. This epic tracks them.

The two P0 children — boolean composition and array containment — ship together in the FIRST PR, because both change the shape of `Filter`/`Predicate` and therefore the HTTP and MCP wire format. Everything else that touches filters must land after them or pay the migration twice.
design: Judged against turbopuffer's documented query + schema surface (docs/query, docs/schema, fetched 2026-08-07). Where nidus is already ahead — server-side query embedding, server-side RRF hybrid in one call — no ticket is filed.

title: JS SDK npm publish has failed every release since #66 (OIDC trusted-publisher keyed to the wrong workflow)
description: npm has only @duckedup/nidus 0.1.0, 0.1.1 and 0.2.0 while the crate is at 0.43.0 — the JS SDK has published NOTHING since 2026-07-15. Every release since #66 (b776f39) fails identically: 'npm error 404 Not Found - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/@duckedup%2fnidus'. npm returns 404 rather than 403 for an unauthorized write, so this is an auth failure, not a missing package. Confirmed on 0.40.0, 0.41.0, 0.42.0 and 0.43.0. Provenance signing SUCCEEDS in the same job (the sigstore transparency-log entry is written), so id-token/OIDC is working — it is specifically the registry write that is unauthorized. Not random: it only looks intermittent because release.yml invokes the SDK workflows only when Cargo.toml's version actually bumped, so releases that ship nothing are vacuously green. The Go and Python SDKs are unaffected — Python uses a long-lived PIPY_TOKEN, and JS is the only SDK on OIDC trusted publishing.
design: Root cause: #66 converted sdk-js-release.yml from 'on: push' to 'workflow_call' (needed, because a tag pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN cannot trigger another workflow). npm's docs state that for workflow_call, 'validation checks the calling workflow's name instead of the workflow that actually contains the publish command'. So npm validates against release.yml, while the trusted publisher on npmjs.com is configured for sdk-js-release.yml — a permanent mismatch. The successes before #66 were push-triggered runs where sdk-js-release.yml WAS the entry workflow. Fix is a one-time npmjs.com settings change: set the trusted publisher's workflow to release.yml. Caveat: the workflow_dispatch entry point then mismatches (its caller is itself), so manual dispatch needs either a second trusted-publisher entry or a token fallback. id-token: write is already granted on both parent and child, which npm also requires.
acceptance_criteria: A release publishes @duckedup/nidus at the crate version; npm view @duckedup/nidus versions shows the current crate version.

title: Wire the fuzzy/token/regex predicates through HTTP, CLI, and the SDKs
description:
nidus-m50.9 shipped Fuzzy, ContainsAllTokens, ContainsAnyToken, ContainsTokenSequence, and Regex as library Predicate variants (indices 16-20). They already serialize over the wire via the existing serde derive, so the HTTP/CLI JSON filter format works today with no server change.

What is NOT done, deliberately deferred to avoid a merge conflict with concurrent work in src/server/:
- src/server/dto.rs: doc/example coverage for the new predicate shapes.
- CLI --where docs for the new operators.
- SDK builder functions: sdks/go (Predicate builders + the wire-shape table in filter_test.go), sdks/js, sdks/python.
- docs/ filter reference page.

The wire shape is the standard externally-tagged serde form the other variants use: Fuzzy is a 3-tuple (key, needle, max_edits); the token predicates and Regex are 2-tuples (key, query).

Semantics to mirror in each SDK: SPEC.md sections 7.4 and 7.5. Note MAX_FUZZY_EDITS = 8 is a caller-facing error, and Regex is anchored at both ends.

title: DECISION: a zero-config local embedder, within the build-cost bar
description:
All eight embed providers (voyage, openai, ollama, cohere, gemini, mistral, jina, openai-compat) need an API key or a running daemon. A local memory store that phones a hosted API to write a note is a hard sell for the obvious use case, and it makes 'nidus mcp' non-zero-config no matter how good the transport is.

This is a decision, not a task, because the obvious implementations collide with the dependency bar: ONNX Runtime is exactly the multi-minute native-toolchain dependency nidus exists to avoid. A static-embedding approach (model2vec-style — a token-to-vector table, no inference engine) is pure Rust and cheap to build, at a real cost in embedding quality.

Decide: ship a bundled static embedder, an optional feature-gated one, or nothing.
design: The constraint is explicit in CLAUDE.md and SPEC.md sections 1 and 13.6: the whole-crate clean build stays well under a minute, no bundled C/C++, no heavy toolchain. Feature-gating does not fully escape it — an optional feature that nobody can afford to enable is not a solution. Also weigh model weight distribution: a table shipped in the crate, downloaded on first use, or supplied by the user.
acceptance_criteria: A written decision with the option taken and the reasoning, recorded in SPEC.md. If the answer is a bundled embedder, a follow-up implementation ticket; if the answer is no, the docs say plainly what a user must set up.

title: Near-duplicate suppression on remember
description:
ids are the only dedup key, and an agent writing a memory invents one — so the same fact gets stored repeatedly under different ids, and recall returns the same thing five times in a top-10.

Wanted: an optional similarity check at write time (cosine over the freshly computed embedding against the target collection; above a threshold, update the existing entry instead of inserting a new one). The embedding is already computed on the remember path, so the marginal cost is one search.
acceptance_criteria: remember can detect a near-duplicate and update in place rather than insert; the threshold is configurable and the behaviour is opt-in; the response tells the caller which happened, so the model learns it already knew this.

title: Collection lifecycle from MCP: create and configure without the CLI
description:
There is no create_collection and no set_fts_schema tool. text_search and hybrid_search both require a field declared in the collection's FTS schema — so for a client that only speaks MCP, both tools are dead on arrival until a human runs the CLI against the store first.

Either expose the lifecycle as tools, or have remember create what it needs on first write. The second is friendlier and probably right for the memory use case.
acceptance_criteria: A pure-MCP client can go from an empty store to a working hybrid_search without touching the CLI; whichever route is chosen, the first-write path is covered in tests/e2e/mcp.rs.

title: Recency: timestamp stamping and TTL for stored memories
description:
Nothing records when a memory was written or last touched, and nothing expires. A note from two years ago is indistinguishable from this morning's, and on pure cosine it wins just as often.

Wanted: created_at and updated_at stamped automatically on remember, and an optional TTL after which an entry stops being recalled. Ranking by age is the sibling ticket on the search epic; this one is the data it needs.
design: Stamping is only half of it — decide whether TTL expiry is enforced at read time (filter the recall) or at compaction (actually reclaim the row), and say so. An epoch Int works today; a real datetime type is the sibling ticket on the search epic.
acceptance_criteria: remember stamps creation and update times without the caller passing them; a TTL can be set per entry or per collection; expired entries stop surfacing in recall and their reclamation behaviour is documented.

title: Projection: include_attributes / exclude_attributes
description:
`Hit` always carries every attr of a matched record. For a memory store whose records hold long text bodies, that is a real payload cost on every search over HTTP — a top-50 recall ships fifty full documents when the caller wanted ids and scores.

turbopuffer has include_attributes and exclude_attributes.
acceptance_criteria: A search can request a named subset of attrs, or all-but-a-named-set; the default (all attrs) is unchanged; the saving is visible in the response size for a large-body collection.
close_reason: Shipped together: SearchOpts::exact forces the exact brute-force scan per query (bypassing the ANN walk, the per-segment IVF fan-out, and the quantized first pass), and Projection::{All,Include,Exclude} on SearchOpts/ListOpts selects the attrs a Hit carries, applied where hits are materialized (hits_from_topk + the list tail) so an excluded attr is never cloned. Wired through HTTP (exact, include_attributes, exclude_attributes on /search; the projection pair on /list; both-set is a 400), the CLI (--exact, --include-attr, --exclude-attr), and all three SDKs. Both default to today's behaviour.

title: Search pagination: continue past the first top_k
description:
`list` takes offset and limit, but `search`, `text_search`, and `hybrid_search` return a top-k with no continuation — to see results 51-100 the caller re-runs with top_k=100 and discards the first fifty.

turbopuffer supports filter-based and offset-style pagination up to a 10k limit.
design: An offset/limit pair over the scored set is the cheap version and is probably enough. A cursor is only worth it if it can be made stable across concurrent writes; given the refresh model, decide whether stability is promised or explicitly not.
acceptance_criteria: Scored searches accept a continuation; the semantics under concurrent writes are documented rather than implied.
close_reason: Shipped offset/limit pagination across every scored surface. SearchOpts and HybridOpts gain offset (default 0); RecallOpts deliberately does not (nidus-m50.15). Store::search's four early-return branches are consolidated into a single tail: each branch ranks offset+top_k deep and ONE paginate() call cuts the page, after the top-k cap. TopK's ordering is now a total order — (score desc, collection, id), applied inside the heap so which of two tied docs survives the k boundary no longer depends on scan order; stated as a contract in SPEC section 7 because later tickets depend on it. Hybrid pages the fused ranking, never a leg. offset+top_k above MAX_TOP_K is a 400 at the HTTP boundary, not a clamp; an offset past the end is an empty page, not an error. Wired through HTTP, the CLI (--offset), and all three SDKs as an optional additive field; nothing added to MCP. SPEC section 7, guides/search.md, reference/api.md and reference/http-api.md updated.

title: Aggregation and result diversity: count, sum, group_by, per-key limit
description:
nidus has no aggregation. Counting matching records means listing them; there is no group_by and no way to cap how many hits come from one attribute value.

turbopuffer has Count, Sum, group_by with ForEachUnique, and limit.per. The per-key cap is the one that matters most here: 'at most 2 hits per file' stops a single verbose document from filling the entire recall window.
acceptance_criteria: Count and Sum over a filter without materialising records; a per-attribute-value cap on results; group_by returning aggregates per value.

title: Result annotations: text highlighting and per-leg scores
description:
A `Hit` carries one fused score and the whole attrs map. A caller cannot see why a hit matched: which BM25 clause fired, what the vector distance was, or which span of the text matched.

turbopuffer returns computed per-result values — VectorDist, BM25, and Highlight with fragment options. For a memory store the snippet is what makes a recall result readable to an agent instead of a wall of stored text.
acceptance_criteria: A hybrid hit can report its vector and BM25 sub-scores; a text or hybrid hit can return highlighted fragments around the matched terms; both are opt-in so the default response size does not grow.

title: a_refused_query_is_not_counted_as_a_served_one races on the global metrics counter
description: src/store/tests.rs:4605 reads the process-global search_queries counter, runs one refused search, and asserts the counter is unchanged. METRICS is a static (src/metrics.rs:237) and src/store/read.rs:309 increments it on every SUCCESSFUL search, while cargo runs the lib tests concurrently — so any sibling test's successful search inside the before/after window fails the assert_eq spuriously. Introduced with the test in #69. Surfaced on PR #73 (unrelated: an IGlob predicate), which touches none of metrics.rs, store/read.rs or store/tests.rs. Only the test-ingest lane fails because --features memory,embed-all,summarize-all compiles 85 extra lib tests (594 vs 509), including src/memory.rs recall tests that search successfully — more concurrent writers than the plain test lane has.
design: Keep the assertion but make the observation sound. A zero delta PROVES the refused path did not increment, since concurrent noise can only raise the delta; a non-zero delta is ambiguous. So retry the before/after window and pass on the first clean one, failing only if every window moved: a genuine regression increments in every window and still fails deterministically, while transient noise clears. No serialization, no new test binary, no per-store metrics refactor. The sibling pattern at src/server/mod.rs:1719 asserts '> before' and is already monotonic-safe — leave it.
acceptance_criteria: The test passes on the ingest lane; a deliberately reintroduced inc() on the refused path still fails it.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #73: the test now retries the before/after window and passes on the first clean one. Verified it still fails deterministically when the inc() is moved above the refusal check.

title: IGlob: case-insensitive glob predicate
description: nidus's glob matcher is case-sensitive only, so callers that need case-insensitive path matching must hand-roll a character-class rewrite (src/Fin -> [Ss][Rr][Cc]/[Ff][Ii][Nn]), a 4x pattern-size hack. See duckedup/wdpkr#54, which does exactly this and documents nidus's lack of a case-insensitive mode as the reason. Add Predicate::IGlob(key, pattern) — ASCII-case-insensitive glob, mirroring Turbopuffer's IGlob — across the library, HTTP wire, MCP tool schemas, all three SDKs, SPEC 7.1 and the docs.
design: Fold both pattern and text with to_ascii_lowercase while the matcher already collects them into Vec<char>, then reuse the existing match_pattern. Zero extra allocations vs Glob, and no second matcher code path: ASCII lowercasing is a per-char map that leaves every glob metacharacter (* ? [ ] ! ^ -) untouched, so pattern structure is preserved and [A-Z] folds to [a-z] correctly. ASCII-only fold keeps the same pattern meaning on every machine (no locale dependence).
acceptance_criteria: IGlob matches regardless of ASCII case; non-ASCII is passthrough (unfolded); wire format {"IGlob":[key,pattern]} round-trips in all three SDKs; MCP filter schema documents it; just ci + ci-cli + test-e2e clean.
close_reason: Shipped Predicate::IGlob: ASCII-case-insensitive glob across the library, HTTP wire, CLI --where help, all three SDKs, SPEC 7.1 and the docs. Downstream (duckedup/wdpkr#54) can drop its character-class rewrite.

title: Trim every comment to the 3-line cap across the codebase
description:
CLAUDE.md now caps comments at 3 lines (added in the MCP PR). The existing codebase predates that rule and violates it in ~500 places across 85 files.

Worst offenders: src/store/mod.rs (48 blocks), src/server/mod.rs (48), src/store/read.rs (22), src/backend/object.rs (22), src/store/write.rs (19), src/backend/mod.rs (19), src/cli/mod.rs (18), tests/e2e/cluster.rs (15), src/store/tests.rs (15), src/lib.rs (14).

Separate from the MCP PR on purpose: 85 files of comment churn mixed into a feature diff makes both unreviewable.

Keep the fact, drop the argument. What gets cut: restatements of the code, multi-paragraph design justification, arguing with an imagined reviewer, the history of how a decision was reached. What stays: the non-obvious why, a constraint that will bite, a bug being guarded against. Rationale worth more than three lines moves to SPEC.md or a bd issue rather than being deleted outright — several of these comments are the only written record of a real decision.

NOT mechanical — every trim needs the comment read and understood, so no regex sweep. Behaviour must not change: no code edits, and the full gate suite stays green.
acceptance_criteria: Every //, ///, and //! block in git-tracked .rs files is 3 lines or fewer, counting the whole block including /// separators. just ci, ci-cli, ci-serve green. No functional code changed — the diff is comments only.
notes:
PROGRESS: src/store/mod.rs done (48 -> 0), commit 3bda9bc on branch comment-cap.

Method that works: dump oversized blocks with the awk one-liner below, read them, then batch-replace via a python script with explicit old->new pairs (exact-match asserts catch drift). Verify with cargo check plus a diff check that zero non-comment lines changed.

  awk 'BEGIN{n=0;s=0} /^[[:space:]]*(\/\/|\/\/\/|\/\/!)/{if(n==0)s=NR;n++;buf=buf $0"\n";next} {if(n>3){print "@@@ "s; printf "%s", buf} n=0;buf=""} END{if(n>3){print "@@@ "s; printf "%s", buf}}' FILE

Ranked remainder: server/mod.rs 48, store/read.rs 22, backend/object.rs 22, store/write.rs 19, backend/mod.rs 19, cli/mod.rs 18, e2e/cluster.rs 15, store/tests.rs 15, lib.rs 14, config.rs 13, server/metrics.rs 12, server/limits.rs 12, model.rs 12, data/mod.rs 11, benchmarks/src/write.rs 11, data/segments.rs 10, then a long tail of <10.

title: MCP 2026-07-28 server surface over the memory layer
description:
Expose nidus as an MCP server so any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, ...) can use the shipped memory layer as agent memory with zero glue code.

WHY NOW: MCP 2026-07-28 removed protocol-level sessions, the initialize/initialized handshake, the held-open HTTP GET stream, and per-connection list results; method/tool names moved to Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers. That stateless request/response model maps onto the existing axum router without distorting it. Pre-2.0 MCP required session affinity, which would have fought the cluster mode where standby writers answer 503 so a load balancer routes around them.

WHY IT FITS: the memory layer is already shipped and is the front-page identity (docs tagline: "Remember text, recall the relevant bits"), and index.mdx names agent memory as a target use case. Memory::remember/recall are text-in/text-out, so they are directly LLM-callable. MCP is the missing front door, not a new direction.

Starting clean on 2.0 means zero migration debt: every deprecation in the release (Roots, Sampling, Logging, HTTP+SSE, DCR) is something nidus would never implement.
design:
DECIDED: use rmcp 3.1.1 (pinned), NOT a hand-rolled implementation.

Hand-rolling was evaluated and rejected. The 2.0 core is small enough to hand-roll (JSON-RPC dispatch, server/discover, tools/list, tools/call, header validation), and codebase precedent favours it (crc.rs is a hand-rolled CRC32; auth.rs hand-rolls constant-time compare rather than taking subtle). But that precedent breaks here: CRC32 and constant-time compare are FROZEN specs, while MCP has revised three times in eighteen months and now ships a formal twelve-month deprecation treadmill. The hard part that survives 2.0 is the version matrix, and it is real in rmcp: ProtocolVersion::KNOWN_VERSIONS with V_2025_11_25 and V_2026_07_28, NegotiatingStatelessHttpService still handling InitializeRequest and negotiating down, missing_required_keys gating the new required _meta on < V_2026_07_28. Hand-rolling means either 2.0-only (talking to almost no client deployed today) or reimplementing sessions + SSE + handshake + negotiation.

COST (measured, not estimated): 27 marginal crates vs the existing --features cli tree of 163, all pure Rust, no C/FFI, ~4.3s cold build. cli-gated, so the default library build, cargo add nidus, just deps, and the build-thesis dep-absence guard are all untouched by construction. Roughly a third to a half of those crates are schemars schema-derivation machinery; we do NOT derive - schemas are hand-written JSON literals, which keeps description wording under our control (it drives tool-selection quality more than anything else).

SHAPE: adapter over the library, per the binary-adapts-to-the-library rule. StreamableHttpService implements tower_service::Service<Request<B>> with Error = Infallible, and axum Extension state reaches the handlers (tower.rs:976), so it nests as:
  router.nest_service("/mcp", StreamableHttpService::new(|| Ok(NidusMcp::new(state.clone())), NeverSessionManager::default(), cfg))
under the existing auth middleware and body-limit layer. rmcp does not want to own the router.

TOOL SURFACE: remember, recall, text_search, hybrid_search, list_collections, stats. The raw vector routes stay OFF the MCP surface - no model can emit a 384-float array as a tool argument. This means MCP is only useful with the memory feature, so the mcp feature folds into serve.

SKIP ENTIRELY: Tasks, MRTR, subscriptions, resources, prompts, OAuth/CIMD, sampling, roots, logging. Every nidus op is a fast synchronous call; compact is the only slow one and is not agent-facing. Authorization reuses the existing constant-time bearer token - the spec does not force OAuth, and bearer + localhost is the right model for a dev/small-scale store.

GOTCHA: rmcp own comment at tower.rs:856 notes axum::Router::nest can drop the Host header hyper synthesizes. Assert this in the e2e lane rather than discovering it in the field.
acceptance_criteria: nidus serve exposes a working MCP endpoint at /mcp speaking 2026-07-28 statelessly; tools/list and tools/call work from a real MCP client; e2e tests cover the real bind and the Host-header-through-nest case; default build dep tree unchanged; docs describe the feature present-tense.
close_reason: Closed

title: Docs sidebar active link flickers/lags during view-transition navigation
description: The custom docs Sidebar (position:fixed) was captured in Astro ClientRouter's full-page ::view-transition-old/new(root) crossfade. During the ~200ms crossfade the browser paints a snapshot of the OLD sidebar (old active link + old TOC) fading out over the correct new DOM, producing a double-image where two links appear active. With rapid clicks Chrome can leave a stale frame, so the active link appears not to update (hit or miss). Fix: add transition:animate="none" to the sidebar <nav> so it becomes its own non-animated view-transition group and swaps instantly, out of the root crossfade.

title: Index the fuzzy/token text predicates instead of rescanning per record
description:
The predicates added in nidus-m50.9 (Fuzzy, ContainsAllTokens, ContainsAnyToken, ContainsTokenSequence, Regex) have no index behind them. Each is evaluated per scanned record against the raw attribute:

- token predicates: re-tokenize the attribute, O(attribute length) per row
- Fuzzy: a two-row Levenshtein DP, O(needle x attribute) per row (skipped when the length gap exceeds the budget)
- Regex: compiled once per query (cached by pattern), then a linear-time match per row

This is stated in SPEC.md section 7.4 so it is not discovered in production. It is fine at nidus's target scale and it is the wrong shape for a large corpus.

Options if this becomes a bottleneck: reuse the FTS inverted index for the token predicates when the field happens to be FTS-indexed (the analyzers differ - filter tokens are unstemmed - so this needs a raw-token posting list, not the stemmed one); an n-gram or BK-tree index for Fuzzy; a literal-prefix extraction pass for Regex to narrow candidates. All are additive over the same on-disk format.

Do not build until a real workload demands it.

title: CLI set-fts-schema applies its tuning flags to every --field at once
description: src/cli/mod.rs's set-fts-schema takes --k1/--b/--ascii-folding/--max-token-len as invocation-wide flags, so a caller who wants different BM25 params for 'title' and 'body' cannot express it from the CLI (the library, HTTP API, and all three SDKs are per-field). Options: a --field-spec 'body:k1=1.5,b=0.3' form, or accepting a JSON array. Low priority — the HTTP surface covers the case today. Shipped alongside nidus-m50.13.

title: Docs: the auto-capture hook recipe for agent memory
description:
Even with every tool in place, memory only gets written when the model remembers to call remember — which is exactly the failure mode a memory store exists to fix. What makes it automatic is host-side wiring: a session-start hook that recalls relevant context, a stop hook that writes back what was learned.

None of that is nidus code, and all of it is missing from the docs. This is the ticket that makes the rest of the epic land for a real user.
design: Keep to the documented positioning: describe what nidus does today, neutrally, without pinning it down as one deployment shape or promising future modes.
acceptance_criteria: A docs page walking from an empty store to working automatic memory: registering the stdio server, the hook configuration, the collection and attr conventions that make later filtering work, and a worked recall example.

title: MCP resources and prompts alongside the tool surface
description:
nidus exposes tools only. MCP also has resources and prompts.

Resources would make stored memories addressable and mentionable directly rather than reachable only through a tool call — a collection as a browsable resource, an entry as a URI. Prompts could ship the recall-then-answer pattern with the server instead of leaving each client to invent it.
acceptance_criteria: Collections and entries are exposed as MCP resources with stable URIs; at least one prompt ships the intended recall pattern; both stay text-native and route through the existing helpers.

title: Expose BM25 tuning and analyzer configuration in the FTS schema
description:
K1 (1.2) and B (0.75) are hard-coded consts in src/fts/mod.rs, there is no k3, and `Language` has exactly one variant (English) gating the stopword set and Porter stemmer.

turbopuffer exposes k1, b, k3, the tokenizer, ASCII folding, case sensitivity, and max token length per field. Nothing here is wrong as a default — the gap is that a caller indexing code identifiers or a non-English corpus cannot change it.
design: Note that K1 is already mixed into the index cache key (src/fts/mod.rs), so making it per-field has an existing seam to respect — a schema change must invalidate cached indexes.
acceptance_criteria: k1 and b are settable per FTS field with today's values as defaults; the cache key accounts for them; adding a second Language is possible without touching call sites.
close_reason: Per-field FtsField { field, k1, b, Analyzer { language, ascii_folding, max_token_len } } replaces the store-wide K1/B consts; defaults are bit-identical (frozen-score tests). New Op::SetFtsFields appended LAST (variant 7); legacy SetFtsSchema still replays with defaults. FTS cache key bumped to v2 and now serializes the whole schema, so any param change rebuilds. Wired through lib API, HTTP (untagged name-or-object field entries), CLI flags, and all three SDKs. 36 new Rust tests + SDK tests; ci, ci-cli, integration, e2e, miri green.

title: Per-query choice of ANN vs exact search
description:
`Config::ann` is a store-level setting: a store either has an index or it does not, and every query takes the same path. turbopuffer picks ANN or exact kNN per query.

The useful case is a caller who wants a guaranteed-exact answer for a small filtered subset while keeping the index for everything else.
acceptance_criteria: A single query can force the exact path on an ANN-configured store, and the choice is exposed over HTTP and the SDKs.
close_reason: Shipped together: SearchOpts::exact forces the exact brute-force scan per query (bypassing the ANN walk, the per-segment IVF fan-out, and the quantized first pass), and Projection::{All,Include,Exclude} on SearchOpts/ListOpts selects the attrs a Hit carries, applied where hits are materialized (hits_from_topk + the list tail) so an excluded attr is never cloned. Wired through HTTP (exact, include_attributes, exclude_attributes on /search; the projection pair on /list; both-set is a 400), the CLI (--exact, --include-attr, --exclude-attr), and all three SDKs. Both default to today's behaviour.

title: Multi-query batching in one request
description:
One query per request today. turbopuffer accepts up to 16 simultaneous queries with optional RRF reranking across them.

For an agent this saves round-trips when fanning one question into several phrasings — and the fusion machinery already exists, since hybrid_search fuses two legs with RRF.
acceptance_criteria: A batch of queries is answerable in one HTTP call; optional cross-query RRF reuses the existing fusion code; the batch is bounded and counted against the existing backpressure limits.

title: Multi-field BM25: combine several text clauses
description:
`FtsQuery` names exactly one field, and `hybrid_search` is exactly one vector leg plus one BM25 field. A record with both a title and a body cannot be searched across both in one query.

turbopuffer combines multiple BM25 clauses with Sum and Max, nestable.
acceptance_criteria: A text or hybrid search can name several FTS fields and combine their scores; single-field queries are unchanged.

title: Text predicates: regex, fuzzy, and token operators
description:
Filter-side text matching is Glob and IGlob only. turbopuffer additionally has Regex, Fuzzy (Levenshtein), and the token family ContainsAllTokens / ContainsTokenSequence / ContainsAnyToken with prefix support.

Fuzzy is the interesting one for a memory store — an agent recalling a half-remembered identifier. Regex brings a dependency and a ReDoS question, so treat it as a separate decision.
acceptance_criteria: Fuzzy and the token operators are available as predicates; if regex is adopted, the engine choice and its worst-case behaviour are recorded first.
close_reason: Shipped Fuzzy (ASCII-case-folded Levenshtein, MAX_FUZZY_EDITS=8 as a caller-facing error), ContainsAllTokens/ContainsAnyToken/ContainsTokenSequence over a self-contained unstemmed tokenizer, and Regex on the regex crate (anchored both ends; linear-time FA engine so no ReDoS guard needed; compiled once per query into a capped cache). Predicate variants 16-20, appended last, with a variant-index back-compat test. Clean build 11.4s -> 11.6s (lib) and 14.5s -> 15.1s (--features cli), inside the build-cost bar. SPEC 7.4/7.5 record the semantics and the per-record scan cost. Wire/SDK surface deferred to nidus-icn; indexing to nidus-1ba.

title: Document the MCP endpoint and bump the version
description:
Add a docs guide for the MCP endpoint (config, client wiring, the tool list) and cross-link it from the memory guide, since MCP is that layer front door.

Describe it PRESENT-TENSE only. Per the docs positioning rule: no roadmap promises, no "planned", and do not pin nidus down as a library-not-a-server.

Bump Cargo.toml version (minor - new feature). Leave charts/nidus/Chart.yaml alone (stamped by helm-publish at release time) and leave the SDK manifests alone (stamped from Cargo.toml at release time). Only touch the install snippets in getting-started.md and README.md if major.minor changed.
close_reason: Closed

title: ANN: exact-prefilter for selective filters
description: The v1 post-filter is silently lossy when a filter/scope is selective (graph walk starves before enough matching candidates surface). Add an exact-prefilter path (or adaptive ef widening) so filtered ANN queries keep recall. Follow-up to nidus-nhc.
close_reason: ANN exact-prefilter for selective filters (read.rs search_ann) + store/mod.rs split into scoring/quant/read/write/tests submodules; CLAUDE.md gains a 'keep files focused' convention. just ci + ci-cli + miri all green.

title: ANN: CLI/server flags to configure ann
description: Expose Config::ann through the cli feature: nidus serve / cli open flags for ann kind + params; mirror in server/dto.rs if surfaced over HTTP. Follow-up to nidus-nhc.
close_reason: Exposed Config::ann through the cli feature: --ann <hnsw|ivf> plus per-knob flags (--ann-m/-ef-construction/-ef-search/-n-lists/-n-probe/-overscan/-seed) on the shared StoreArgs, so every store-opening command (incl. serve) can build/consult the index. ANN is open-time config (not in the header), so it's passed per open. Active config echoed via GET /stats and nidus stats through a shared AnnDto (server/dto.rs). Tests + docs (cli-and-server, http-server) updated; version 0.12.1.

title: ANN: combine with quantization (quantized walk + f32 rerank)
description: Lift the v1 mutual-exclusion: build the ANN graph/lists using quantized (int8/binary) distances for the cheap walk, then f32 rerank candidates. More recall tuning required. Follow-up to nidus-nhc.
close_reason: Quantized ANN walk + f32 rerank: lifted ann/quant mutual-exclusion; Walk abstraction scores int8/binary codes during HNSW build+search and IVF list scans (centroids stay f32), store reranks candidates exactly. Cache validity keyed on quant kind. Shipped in 0.13.0.

title: Exotic vector types: sparse, multi-vector late interaction, f16
description:
nidus is one dense vector per record with one dimension pinned per store. int8 and binary quantization exist but are store-wide, not per-attribute.

turbopuffer has sparse vectors with SparseKNN, multi-vector late interaction (ColBERT-style) over vector arrays, and f16 alongside f32 and i8.

Filed for completeness of the survey. This is the largest change on the list and the least justified by the memory use case — it touches the data segment format, not just the query path. Do not start without a design decision first.
acceptance_criteria: None yet — this is a placeholder for a design decision, not scheduled work.
close_reason: DECIDED, shipped as SPEC §9 decision text. f16 REJECTED (int8 quant already beats it 4x with rerank; a third storage width multiplies the codec/scan/quant matrix for a worse trade). Multi-vector late interaction DEFERRED as rerank-only — needs no format change if scoped that way. Sparse DEFERRED: format could carry it additively but the surround is out of proportion — breaking Record change, second Op append, working-set key bump discarding every deployed memtier snapshot, payload held twice outside max_vector_bytes, no worst-case bound on a common-dimension query, and no named caller. 'Not yet', not 'never'.

value: Docs site (docs/) builds with bun, not npm: system node is v22.11 (too old for Astro, needs >=22.12). bun is installed at ~/.bun/bin/bun but isn't on the non-interactive shell PATH. Build with: ~/.bun/bin/bun --bun run build (the --bun flag forces bun's runtime so astro doesn't shell out to the old system node). Files in docs/public/ are copied verbatim to dist/ root (e.g. llms.txt served at site root).
